Chapter 1: Math

1 Math

1.1 Notation

  • (Loose) Einstein Summation notation is used in which if an index appears twice in both top and bottom, such as 𝜕𝜇𝜕𝜇, it is equivalent to summing over said indices such as ∑𝜇∈{0,1,2,3}𝜕𝜇𝜕𝜇

    • The reason that this is loose is due to the fact that if two indices appear twice in an expression but they are both on the bottom, it is implied that the reader should raise the second appearance of the index. The following is an example so the reader doesn’t get confused: 𝜕𝜇𝜕𝜇=𝜕𝜇𝜕𝜇=∑𝜇∈{0,1,2,3}𝜕𝜇𝜕𝜇

  • The Dirac Delta Function is defined as

    𝛿(𝑥)≡dd𝑥𝐻(𝑥)

    with

    ∫𝑑𝑥 𝛿(𝑥)=1

This is not, in fact, a function, due to its unorthodox definition. Instead, it is a distribution (it can be defined as the limit of several different distributions, such as the normal distribution, a uniform distribution, etc.).

  • 𝑥⃗=𝑥𝑖, 𝑖∈{1,2,3} (spatial components of 𝑥)
  • The d’Alembertian operator □≡𝜕𝜇𝜕𝜇

This operator is useful in Lagrangians and the Klein-Gordon equation.

  • The Laplacian operator △≡𝜕𝑖𝜕𝑖 where 𝑖∈{1,2,3}

  • Natural Units are used in which ℏ=𝑐 =1

  • Both Sided Derivative: 𝜙∗𝜕𝜇⃡𝜙≡(𝜙∗𝜕𝜇𝜙−𝜙𝜕𝜇𝜙∗)

  • Feynman Slash: 𝑝≡𝑝𝜇𝛾𝜇

  • Pauli matrices

𝜎0=(11),𝜎1=(11),𝜎2=(−𝑖𝑖),𝜎3=(1−1)

and 𝜎𝜇≡(𝜎0,𝜎⃗), 𝜎̄𝜇≡(𝜎0,−𝜎⃗)

  • 𝛾𝜇=(𝜎𝜇𝜎̄𝜇)

    in the Weyl representation

  • 𝜓̄≡𝜓†𝛾0 where 𝜓 is a Dirac spinor

  • Left Handed Derivative

    𝜓̄(−𝑖𝜕⃖−𝑚)=−𝑖𝜕𝜇𝜓̄𝛾𝜇−𝑚𝜓̄

    (Derivative acts on the left)

  • 𝑘𝜇2≡𝑘𝜇𝑘𝜇

  • 𝜓𝛼 left handed Weyl spinor

  • 𝜓̃𝛼̇ right handed Weyl spinor

  • 𝜓=(𝜓𝛼𝜒̃𝛽̇) Dirac spinor (Representation of (12,0)⊕(0,12))

All of these expressions regarding spinors will be explained or will quickly become evident in Section 2, due to the complexity of their structure.

1.3 Group Theory

Definition 1.3.1.

A Group 𝐺 is a set of elements {𝑔𝑖}∈𝐺 and a rule 𝑔𝑖×𝑔𝑗=𝑔𝑘 giving how they “multiply.”

1.3.1 Group Theory Axioms

  • For each element 𝑔𝑖∈𝐺 and 𝑔𝑗∈𝐺, their product 𝑔𝑖×𝑔𝑗=𝑔𝑘∈𝐺 is an element of 𝐺

  • Products must be Associative:

    (𝑔𝑖×𝑔𝑗)×𝑔𝑘=𝑔𝑖×(𝑔𝑗×𝑔𝑘)

  • There must be an Identity:

    𝟙×𝑔𝑖=𝑔𝑖×𝟙=𝑔𝑖

  • Elements have an Inverse:

    𝑔𝑖−1×𝑔𝑖=𝟙

Definition 1.3.1.1 (Representation).

An embedding of 𝑔𝑖 as operators in a vector space
  • Matrices are finite-dimensional representations of a group

Definition 1.3.1.2 (Faithful Representation).

Each element in a group gets its own matrix

1.3.2 Lie Groups

  • A Group 𝐺 whose elements can be written as 𝑔𝑖=exp(𝑖𝑐𝑖𝑔𝜆𝑖) for some number 𝑐𝑖𝑔 and some matrix 𝜆𝑖 (known as a generator)

  • In an algebra, you can add and multiply

  • In a Group, you have to follow the previously mentioned rules (just multiplication is allowed)

Definition 1.3.2.1 (Lie Group).

A Lie Group is a type of group with an infinite number of elements and a finite number of generators.

Definition 1.3.2.2 (Lie Algebra).

The Generators of a Lie group form a Lie Algebra.

Example 1.3.2.3 (Lie Algebras).

  • QED : U(1) (unitarity)
  • Weak: SU(2) (special unitarity)
  • Strong: SU(3)
  • Lorent Group: O(1,3) (orthogonal and preserving (1,3) metric) (see §2.2)
